claim: Gut redox potential increased within hours of an antibiotic dose in mice.
source: We showed gut redox potential increased within hours of an antibiotic dose in mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of redox potential in mouse feces during antibiotic treatment.

claim: Within sixteen hours after the first dose of antibiotics, redox potential significantly increased from 37 ± 164 mV at baseline to 227 ± 45 mV (p=0.04 Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U test).
source: Within sixteen hours after the first dose of antibiotics, redox potential significantly increased from 37 ± 164 mV at baseline to 227 ± 45 mV (p=0.04 Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by direct measurements and statistical analysis of redox potential changes.

claim: Throughout treatment, redox potential differed overall between treated and control mice (p=0.005 linear mixed effects model likelihood tests).
source: Throughout treatment, redox potential differed overall between treated and control mice (p=0.005 linear mixed effects model likelihood tests).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of redox measurements across treatment period.

claim: Expression of Nos2 increased relative to controls after antibiotic treatment.
source: We measured increases relative to controls in Nos2, which is linked to reactive nitrogen species levels (Dedon and Tannenbaum, 2004; Winterbourn, 2008); increases relative to controls in Rela, which has been found to contribute to IBD type inflammation in mice via a proinflammatory cytokine response (Waddell et al., 2013); and, decreases relative to controls in Apoa4, which has known anti-inflammatory function (Broedl et al., 2007) (p<0.05, Bonferroni-corrected one-sample t-tests; Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR measurements of gene expression and cited literature on gene function.

claim: Nos2 is linked to reactive nitrogen species levels.
source: We measured increases relative to controls in Nos2, which is linked to reactive nitrogen species levels (Dedon and Tannenbaum, 2004; Winterbourn, 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Rela has been found to contribute to IBD type inflammation in mice via a proinflammatory cytokine response.
source: increases relative to controls in Rela, which has been found to contribute to IBD type inflammation in mice via a proinflammatory cytokine response (Waddell et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Apoa4 has known anti-inflammatory function.
source: decreases relative to controls in Apoa4, which has known anti-inflammatory function (Broedl et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Antibiotic treatment was followed by a small, but significant, decrease in lipocalin-2 levels (p<0.001, linear mixed effects model likelihood tests).
source: Antibiotic treatment was also followed by a small, but significant, decrease in lipocalin-2 levels, which is a protein biomarker of inflammation (Chassaing et al., 2012) (p<0.001, linear mixed effects model likelihood tests; Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: Lipocalin-2 is a protein biomarker of inflammation.
source: lipocalin-2 levels, which is a protein biomarker of inflammation (Chassaing et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Treating an ex vivo human gut system with antibiotics led to an increase in redox potential relative to an untreated control (p=0.005, linear mixed effects model likelihood tests).
source: Treating this system with the same antibiotic cocktail as used in the mouse study led to an increase in redox potential relative to an untreated control (p=0.005, linear mixed effects model likelihood tests; Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by continuous redox measurements in bioreactor system.

claim: Redox potential increased by 59 ± 47 mV within fifteen hours of the first antibiotic dose in the ex vivo system.
source: Redox potential increased by 59 ± 47 mV within fifteen hours of the first antibiotic dose, mirroring the rapidity with which redox shifts occurred in vivo (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by continuous redox measurements in bioreactor.

claim: In the absence of direct interactions between antibiotics and a host, antibiotic treatment produced shifts in environmental redox potential experienced by a gut microbial community.
source: Thus, in the absence of direct interactions between antibiotics and a host, antibiotic treatment produced shifts in environmental redox potential experienced by a gut microbial community.
evidence: Inferred from ex vivo bioreactor experiments that lack host tissue.

claim: Fecal bacterial concentrations decreased significantly within twelve hours of antibiotic treatment (p=0.01, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U test).
source: Fecal bacterial concentrations decreased significantly within twelve hours of antibiotic treatment (p=0.01, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 2B)
evidence: Supported by qPCR measurements of 16S rRNA gene copy number.

claim: Fecal bacterial concentrations remained significantly below controls throughout the five days of treatment (p<0.001, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U tests).
source: and remained significantly below controls throughout the five days of treatment (p<0.001, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U tests; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by qPCR measurements over time.

claim: The short-chain fatty acids propionate and acetate decreased eight hours after antibiotic treatment (p<0.05, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U tests).
source: Using NMR-based metabolomics, we found that the short-chain fatty acids propionate and acetate, end products of key microbial metabolic pathways, decreased eight hours after antibiotic treatment (p<0.05, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U tests; Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by NMR metabolomics measurements.

claim: Twenty-one of twenty-eight metabolites measured decreased significantly under antibiotic treatment (p<0.05, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U tests).
source: Twenty-one of twenty-eight metabolites measured, including other short-chain fatty acids, amino acids, branched-chain amino acids, and a group of bile acids, later decreased significantly under antibiotic treatment (p<0.05, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U tests; Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by NMR metabolomics measurements.

claim: The dynamics of twelve metabolites was significantly associated with treatment overall (p<0.05, linear mixed effects model likelihood tests).
source: The dynamics of twelve of those metabolites was significantly associated with treatment overall (p<0.05, linear mixed effects model likelihood tests; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of metabolomics data.

claim: Luminal oxygen levels significantly increased the day after antibiotic treatment (3.7 ± 3.6 Torr at baseline to 26.5 ± 26.1 Torr; p=0.02, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U test).
source: we observed a significant increase in luminal oxygen levels the day after antibiotic treatment (3.7 ± 3.6 Torr at baseline to 26.5 ± 26.1 Torr; p=0.02, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by in vivo oxygen sensor measurements.

claim: Gut oxygen levels in antibiotic-treated mice returned to control levels by forty-eight hours after the first dose (p>0.05, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U test).
source: However, gut oxygen levels in antibiotic-treated mice returned to control levels by forty-eight hours after the first dose (p>0.05, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U test)
evidence: Supported by in vivo oxygen measurements over time.

claim: Antibiotics were not associated with an overall effect on gut oxygen levels (p>0.05 linear mixed effects model likelihood tests).
source: and antibiotics were not associated with an overall effect on gut oxygen levels (p>0.05 linear mixed effects model likelihood tests).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of oxygen measurements.

claim: Among treated mice, gut oxygen levels were not correlated with redox potential (p>0.05, repeated measures correlation).
source: Moreover, among treated mice, gut oxygen levels were not correlated with redox potential (p>0.05, repeated measures correlation; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical correlation analysis.

claim: There was a significant increase in nitrate beginning less than 24 hr after the first dose of antibiotics (p=0.03, Mann-Whitney U test).
source: We measured fecal nitrate levels with the chromotropic acid method (West and Ramachandran, 1966) for a subset of time points when redox varied, and found a significant increase in nitrate (p=0.03, Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 3B) beginning less than 24 hr after the first dose of antibiotics.
evidence: Supported by colorimetric measurements of nitrate.

claim: The increase in nitrate persisted throughout treatment, and overall antibiotic treatment produced a significant increase in nitrate (p=0.02, linear mixed effects model likelihood tests).
source: This increase persisted throughout treatment, and overall antibiotic treatment produced a significant increase in nitrate (p=0.02, linear mixed effects model likelihood tests).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of nitrate measurements over time.

claim: There was a significant effect of treatment on fumarate levels (p<0.001, linear mixed effects model likelihood tests).
source: Overall, there was a significant effect of treatment on fumarate levels (p<0.001, linear mixed effects model likelihood tests; Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fumarate measurements.

claim: A spike in fumarate levels occurred 4 hr after the first antibiotics dose (p=0.004, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U test).
source: We observed a spike in fumarate levels 4 hr after the first antibiotics dose (p=0.004, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U test)
evidence: Supported by colorimetric enzyme assay measurements.

claim: Later during treatment, a significant decrease (to below the detection limit) in fumarate levels was observed.
source: however, this increase had dissipated by 8 hr after the first dose and later during treatment, we observed a significant decrease (to below the detection limit) in fumarate levels.
evidence: Supported by fumarate measurements over time.

claim: Gut bacterial load recovered rapidly after treatment across all treated mice, exhibiting no difference relative to control mice by two days (p>0.05, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U tests).
source: Gut bacterial load recovered rapidly after treatment across all treated mice, exhibiting no difference relative to control mice by two days (p>0.05, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U tests; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by qPCR measurements during recovery period.

claim: A reproducible recovery of beta-diversity was observed after one week (p>0.05, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U test).
source: A reproducible recovery of beta-diversity was observed after one week (p>0.05, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and beta-diversity analysis.

claim: Three clusters of bacterial genera differed significantly during treatment (p<0.05, linear mixed effects model likelihood tests).
source: Amongst these five groups, three differed significantly during treatment (p<0.05, linear mixed effects model likelihood tests; Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by clustering analysis of 16S rRNA gene sequencing data.

claim: The cluster primarily composed of members of the Enterobacteriaceae remained elevated into the beginning of the recovery period (p<0.05, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U tests).
source: One of these, the cluster primarily composed of members of the Enterobacteriacaeae, remained elevated into the beginning of the recovery period as well (p<0.05, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U tests).
evidence: Supported by clustering analysis of sequencing data during recovery.

claim: Enterobacteriaceae often bloom following antibiotic treatment.
source: This enrichment is in line with previous findings that Enterobacteriaceae often bloom following antibiotic treatment (Antonopoulos et al., 2009; David et al., 2015; Young and Schmidt, 2004; Theriot et al., 2014; Peterfreund et al., 2012; Dethlefsen et al., 2008; Jakobsson et al., 2010; Looft and Allen, 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: By the end of the one week recovery period, the abundance of all clusters was indistinguishable between treated and control animals (p>0.05, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U tests).
source: However, by the end of the one week recovery period, the abundance of all clusters was indistinguishable between treated and control animals (p>0.05, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U tests).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of cluster abundances.

claim: Redox potential returned to control levels within a week after treatment ended (p>0.05, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U tests).
source: Redox potential returned to control levels within a week after treatment ended (p>0.05, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U tests; Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by redox measurements during recovery period.

claim: The day after antibiotic therapy ceased, fecal redox potentials in treated mice were significantly decreased relative to control mice (-138.3 ± 149.8 mV vs 54.6 ± 211 mV; p=0.006, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U test).
source: Notably, though, we observed the day after antibiotic therapy ceased, fecal redox potentials in treated mice were significantly decreased relative to control mice (-138.3 ± 149.8 mV vs 54.6 ± 211 mV; p=0.006, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U test)
evidence: Supported by redox measurements at specific time point.

claim: Oxygen and inflammation biomarker levels remained low throughout the recovery period (p>0.05, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U tests).
source: Oxygen and inflammation biomarker levels remained low throughout the recovery period (p>0.05, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U tests; Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, respectively)
evidence: Supported by oxygen and lipocalin-2 measurements during recovery.

claim: Many microbial metabolic products measured by NMR had recovered two days after the last doses, and all had recovered by the end of the recovery week.
source: Furthermore, many microbial metabolic products measured by NMR had recovered two days after the last doses, and all had recovered by the end of the recovery week (Figure 2—figure supplement 3; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by NMR metabolomics measurements during recovery.

claim: The relative abundance of the Enterobacteriaceae was marginally correlated with redox potential (p=0.1, r=0.18, repeated measures correlation) throughout treatment and recovery.
source: We found that the relative abundance of the Enterobacteriaceae was marginally correlated with redox potential (p=0.1, r=,0.18, repeated measures correlation; Figure 4—figure supplement 3) throughout treatment and recovery.
evidence: Supported by statistical correlation analysis of sequencing and redox data.

claim: The change in redox potential during the earlier recovery period was negatively correlated with changes in Enterobacteriaceae absolute abundance for both treated animals (p=0.03, r = −0.42, repeated measures correlation) and for all animals (p=0.02, r = −0.34, repeated measures correlation).
source: Moreover, the change in redox potential during the earlier recovery period was negatively correlated with changes in Enterobacteriaceae absolute abundance (calculated as total 16S rRNA gene copy number multiplied by relative abundance) for both treated animals (p=0.03, r = −0.42, repeated measures correlation) and for all animals (p=0.02, r = −0.34, repeated measures correlation; Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by statistical correlation analysis during recovery period.

claim: Co-housed mice communities had returned to control composition by the end of the recovery period, with the gut microbiota of treated animals equally dissimilar from baseline as it was for control mice (p>0.05, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U test).
source: For co-housed mice, by the end of the recovery period, the gut microbiota of treated animals was equally dissimilar from baseline as it was for control mice indicating that the community had recovered (p>0.05, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by beta-diversity analysis of sequencing data.

claim: Both fecal redox potential and Enterobacteriaceae levels returned to conventional levels more quickly in co-housed mice than singly housed mice.
source: Both fecal redox potential and Enterobacteriaceae levels also returned to conventional levels more quickly in co-housed mice than singly housed mice (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by comparison of redox and sequencing data between housing conditions.

claim: Singly-housed treated mice continued to be more dissimilar at the end of recovery than singly-housed control mice (p<0.001, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U test).
source: By contrast, singly-housed treated mice continued to be more dissimilar at the end of recovery than singly-housed control mice (p<0.001, Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by beta-diversity analysis of sequencing data.

claim: Redox potential is an important environmental feature affected by both host and microbial actions.
source: Redox potential is an important environmental feature affected by both host and microbial actions.
evidence: Stated as a premise based on the study's findings.

claim: Shifts in redox potentials could be attributed specifically to bacterial suppression in a host-free ex vivo human gut microbiota model.
source: Host and microbial functioning changed under treatment, but shifts in redox potentials could be attributed specifically to bacterial suppression in a host-free ex vivo human gut microbiota model.
evidence: Supported by ex vivo bioreactor experiments showing redox changes without host.

claim: Redox dynamics were linked to blooms of the bacterial family Enterobacteriaceae.
source: Redox dynamics were linked to blooms of the bacterial family Enterobacteriaceae.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between redox and Enterobacteriaceae abundance.

claim: Ecological succession to pre-treatment composition was associated with recovery of gut redox.
source: Ecological succession to pre-treatment composition was associated with recovery of gut redox, but also required dispersal from unaffected gut communities.
evidence: Supported by observations of redox and compositional recovery in co-housed mice.

claim: Dispersal from unaffected gut communities was required for ecological succession to pre-treatment composition.
source: Ecological succession to pre-treatment composition was associated with recovery of gut redox, but also required dispersal from unaffected gut communities.
evidence: Supported by differential recovery between co-housed and singly-housed mice.

claim: Bacterial competition for electron acceptors can be a key ecological factor structuring gut communities.
source: As bacterial competition for electron acceptors can be a key ecological factor structuring gut communities, these results support the potential for manipulating gut microbiota through managing bacterial respiration.
evidence: Inferred from the study's findings on redox dynamics and bacterial succession.

claim: Antibiotics have been found to increase gut epithelium oxygenation as a result of altered microbial composition and metabolic signaling to the host.
source: Specifically, antibiotics have been found to increase gut epithelium oxygenation as a result of altered microbial composition and metabolic signaling to the host (Kelly et al., 2015; Rivera-Chávez et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Host inflammation responses to antibiotic treatment and antibiotic-associated pathogen colonization have been shown to produce electron acceptors and other redox active molecules that cause oxidative stress.
source: In addition, host inflammation responses to antibiotic treatment and antibiotic-associated pathogen colonization have been shown to produce electron acceptors and other redox active molecules that cause oxidative stress (Faber et al., 2016; Winter et al., 2010; 2013; Spees et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A wide range of resident gut bacteria can respire aerobically and anaerobically.
source: Furthermore, the contribution of microbial metabolism to gut redox potential has not been tested, although it is known that a wide range of resident gut bacteria can respire aerobically and anaerobically (Ravcheev and Thiele, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Antibiotic disturbance produces reproducible community succession in the gut following treatment—most notably, a transient bloom in Enterobacteriaceae.
source: Antibiotic disturbance produces reproducible community succession in the gut following treatment—most notably, a transient bloom in Enterobacteriaceae (Antonopoulos et al., 2009; David et al., 2015; Young and Schmidt, 2004; Theriot et al., 2014; Peterfreund et al., 2012; Dethlefsen et al., 2008; Jakobsson et al., 2010; Looft and Allen, 2012)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The Enterobacteriaceae bloom has been ascribed to an increase in oxygen availability.
source: which has been ascribed to an increase in oxygen availability (David et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Passive diffusion of oxygen from the epithelium increases redox potential and stimulates growth of aerobic microbes.
source: Passive diffusion of oxygen from the epithelium increases redox potential and stimulates growth of aerobic microbes (Espey, 2013; Albenberg et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Secretion of redox-active immune molecules such as reactive oxygen species or nitrate is known to be a feature of inflammation that imposes oxidative stress on commensal microbes and can be exploited by select pathogens to colonize the intestine.
source: Secretion of redox-active immune molecules such as reactive oxygen species or nitrate is known to be a feature of inflammation that imposes oxidative stress on commensal microbes and can be exploited by select pathogens to colonize the intestine (Winter et al., 2010; 2013; Faber et al., 2016; Spees et al., 2013; Rivera-Chávez et al., 2016; Kelly et al., 2015; David et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: In free-living microbial communities, variation in available electron acceptors dictates where microbes that employ respiration can thrive.
source: In free-living microbial communities, variation in available electron acceptors dictates where microbes that employ respiration can thrive; the differential microbial metabolism that follows can produce further changes in electron acceptor availability (Morris and Schmidt, 2013; Chen et al., 2017; Noll et al., 2005; Orcutt et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Microbial metabolism has been proposed as a mechanism for low redox potential states in the lung of cystic fibrosis patients.
source: Moreover, microbial metabolism has been proposed as a mechanism for low redox potential states in the lung of cystic fibrosis patients (Cowley et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Singly housed mice treated with antibiotics will exhibit altered community composition for weeks after treatment.
source: Previous research has shown that singly housed mice treated with antibiotics will exhibit altered community composition for weeks after treatment (Antonopoulos et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Mice practice coprophagy (i.e., ingestion of feces).
source: Because mice practice coprophagy (i.e., ingestion of feces), we would expect that co-housing would re-introduce normal commensal microbes to compete with the Enterobacteriaceae and other early successional species thereby reducing their abundance.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of mouse behavior.

claim: Microbial respiration of host sourced electron acceptors acts as a major determinant of redox potential in the gut, in addition to the host production itself.
source: Therefore, we propose microbial respiration of host sourced electron acceptors acts as a major determinant of redox potential in the gut, in addition to the host production itself.
evidence: Proposed based on the study's findings from in vivo and ex vivo experiments.

claim: Electron acceptors are a critical resource normally competed over by the resident bacteria and, as such, are key factors structuring gut microbial ecology.
source: Our findings imply that electron acceptors are a critical resource normally competed over by the resident bacteria and, as such, are key factors structuring gut microbial ecology.
evidence: Inferred from the study's findings on redox dynamics and bacterial succession.

claim: The ability to respire a broad range of electron acceptors is already known to be crucial for pathogens to colonize the intestine.
source: The ability to respire a broad range of electron acceptors is already known to be crucial for pathogens to colonize the intestine (Winter et al., 2010; 2013; Faber et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Pathogen colonization resistance by commensal microbes could be mediated by bacterial competition involving respiratory pathways.
source: If true, this hypothesis would imply that pathogen colonization resistance by commensal microbes could be mediated by bacterial competition involving respiratory pathways.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the study's findings.

claim: Enterobacteriaceae are especially suited to exploiting electron acceptor availability because their diverse repertoire of respiration pathways allow for fast growth rates under a high redox regime.
source: Enterobacteriaceae are especially suited to exploiting electron acceptor availability because their diverse repertoire of respiration pathways (Ravcheev and Thiele, 2014; Jones et al., 2007; 2011) allow for fast growth rates under a high redox regime.
evidence: Inferred from cited literature on Enterobacteriaceae respiration capabilities.

claim: Enterobacteriaceae and respiration pathway genes more generally are more prevalent in inflamed mouse guts.
source: Enterobacteriaceae and respiration pathway genes more generally are also more prevalent in inflamed mouse guts (Hughes et al., 2017), another environment where heightened redox potential is expected.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Under experimental inflammation, Enterobacteriaceae expansion can be prevented by treatment with tungstate, a respiration inhibitor.
source: Under experimental inflammation, though, Enterobacteriaceae expansion can be prevented by treatment with tungstate, a respiration inhibitor (Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Members of the Enterobacteriaceae will produce reducing agents, such as H2S, in response to antibiotic treatment.
source: It has previously been shown that members of the Enterobacteriaceae will produce reducing agents, such as H2S, in response to antibiotic treatment (Shatalin et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Antibiotics are triumphs of modern medicine that have dramatically reduced infectious disease mortality.
source: Antibiotics are triumphs of modern medicine that have dramatically reduced infectious disease mortality (Armstrong et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Antibiotics meaningfully reshape the resident gut microbiota, leaving an imprint that can last for months to years after treatment.
source: But, we are increasingly learning that antibiotics also meaningfully reshape the resident gut microbiota, leaving an imprint that can last for months to years after treatment (Dethlefsen and Relman, 2011; Jakobsson et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Antibiotic treatment predisposes hosts to obesity, food allergy, auto-immune disease, and increased infection risk.
source: and predisposing hosts to obesity (Cho et al., 2012), food allergy (Stefka et al., 2014), auto-immune disease (Russell et al., 2012), and increased infection risk (Stecher et al., 2007; Buffie et al., 2012; Wiström et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Germ-free animals exhibit increased gut redox potential.
source: Indeed, germ-free animals (Phillips et al., 1958; Celesk et al., 1976) and humans suffering from inflammatory diseases (Circu and Aw, 2011) and malnutrition (Million et al., 2016) exhibit increased gut redox potential.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Humans suffering from inflammatory diseases exhibit increased gut redox potential.
source: Indeed, germ-free animals (Phillips et al., 1958; Celesk et al., 1976) and humans suffering from inflammatory diseases (Circu and Aw, 2011) and malnutrition (Million et al., 2016) exhibit increased gut redox potential.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Humans suffering from malnutrition exhibit increased gut redox potential.
source: Indeed, germ-free animals (Phillips et al., 1958; Celesk et al., 1976) and humans suffering from inflammatory diseases (Circu and Aw, 2011) and malnutrition (Million et al., 2016) exhibit increased gut redox potential.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The redox electrode has a detection limit of 0.10 mV.
source: The electrode has a detection limit of 0.10 mV (Pang and Zhang, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature on electrode specifications.

claim: The current oxygen sensing system measures lifetime to within 2 µs or better, which equates to ~1 µM O2 at physiological oxygen conditions.
source: The current oxygen sensing system measures lifetime to within 2 µs or better, which equates to ~1 µM O2 at physiological oxygen conditions.
evidence: Technical specification of the oxygen sensor system used.

claim: Baseline microbiome is expected to differ between mouse litters over time as well as between vendor.
source: Because baseline microbiome is expected to differ between mouse litters over time as well as between vendor (Rosshart et al., 2017; Rausch et al., 2016; Ivanov et al., 2009; Campbell et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: There were significant differences between cohorts in their microbiome at the OTU level throughout the experiment (p<0.01, R2 = 0.17, PERMANOVA).
source: An overall analysis of beta-diversity showed that there were significant differences between cohorts in their microbiome at the OTU level throughout the experiment (p<0.01, R2 = 0.17, PERMANOVA; Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of 16S rRNA gene sequencing data from two cohorts.

claim: The cohort effect did not significantly interact with the treatment effect (p=0.3).
source: This cohort effect did not significantly interact with the treatment effect, however (p=0.3).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of cohort and treatment effects.

claim: The Enterobacteriaceae bloom response to antibiotics has been found to be consistent between humans and mice, as well as between mouse vendors.
source: Because the Enterobacteriaceae bloom response to antibiotics has been found to be consistent between humans and mice, as well as between mouse vendors (Antonopoulos et al., 2009; David et al., 2015; Young and Schmidt, 2004; Theriot et al., 2014; Peterfreund et al., 2012; Dethlefsen et al., 2008; Jakobsson et al., 2010; Looft and Allen, 2012)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Male C57BL/6 mice 8–10 weeks of age with a native microbiota were used for all experiments.
source: Male C57BL/6 mice (Charles River Laboratories, Wilmington MA) 8–10 weeks of age with a native microbiota were used for all experiments.
evidence: Description of experimental subjects.

claim: The antibiotic cocktail consisted of ampicillin 1 mg/ml, vancomycin 5 mg/ml, neomycin 10 mg/ml, and metronidazole 10 mg/ml.
source: The antibiotic cocktail consisted of ampicillin (Gold Biotechnology, St. Louis MO) 1 mg/ml, vancomycin (Alfa Aesar, Ward Hill MA) 5 mg/ml, neomycin (EMD Millipore, Burlington MA) 10 mg/ml, and metronidazole (Alfa Aesar) 10 mg/ml (after Reikvam et al., 2011).
evidence: Description of experimental treatment with citation to source protocol.

claim: Gut microbiota were cultured from human stool in a flow-through bioreactor system following previous work.
source: Gut microbiota were cultured from human stool in a flow-through bioreactor system (Infors, Bottmingen Switzerland) following previous work (McDonald et al., 2013).
evidence: Description of ex vivo experimental method with citation.

claim: Healthy human subjects (n = 3) that self-reported no use of antibiotics within a month of enrollment provided a single donation of stool.
source: Healthy human subjects (n = 3) that self-reported no use of antibiotics within a month of enrollment provided a single donation of stool.
evidence: Description of human subjects for ex vivo experiments.

claim: All bioreactor vessels had a total vessel volume of 400 ml and a continuous turnover of 400 ml per day for the media to emulate the 24 hr average passage time of the human gut.
source: All bioreactor vessels had a total vessel volume of 400 ml and a continuous turnover of 400 ml per day for the media to emulate the 24 hr average passage time of the human gut.
evidence: Description of bioreactor experimental conditions.
